test/e2e-record-spec-pointers.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-10-11 — the suite has no principal. It opens the record contracts a `spec` field names (GET /v1/specs/{name}, the /docs/specs/ redirect, /v1/spec, /v1/tracked-responses/spec) with no credentials, because a node or an AI reading someone's record must be able to open what it follows. The documents are the same for every caller by design, so there is no second principal whose answer could differ. The fence it does assert is that a name outside the public contracts (PUBLIC_CONTRACTS in services/contract-docs.ts, five since 2026-10-11) answers 404, and that a path climbing out of docs/specs does too.

test/e2e-seo-noindex.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-30 — the suite has no principal. It reads the node the way an anonymous crawler does (HEAD and GET with the bingbot user agent, no credentials) and asserts the X-Robots-Tag and the robots meta each response carries. The header is the same for every caller by design, so there is no second principal whose answer could differ, and no refusal to assert.

test/e2e-boot-port-in-use.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-17 — the suite has no principal at all. It starts a node on a port another listener already holds and asserts the process exits with the port and the cause named, instead of printing its start banner over the failed listen (docs/pitfalls.md §105). test/e2e-oauth-login.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-04 — in the standard test config no provider is configured, so every authorize and callback answers 503 before any principal question can be reached. That is the suite's purpose against a running node: prove the routes are MOUNTED and gated rather than 404, which is the failure a mounting mistake produces and which no unit test can see. The refusals that involve an identity — an unmapped subject, a state that does not match, a session issued to the wrong account — need a working IdP and are covered by test/unit/oauth-login.test.ts against a fake one.

test/e2e-portfolio-origin.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-04 — the portfolio origin is a public vanity host: <username>.portfolio.<apex> serves whatever that owner chose to publish, to anyone, with no session anywhere in the flow. The suite self-spawns a node with the origin provisioned because the shared runner keeps the flag off. Its refusals are host-shaped and asserted four times over, all as the same 404: an account that has not published yet, a username no account holds, a reserved label ('www'), and an owner who set enabled:false. One answer for all four, so the host cannot be used to find out which usernames exist. There is no door here for a second principal to be refused at. test/e2e-registration-invites.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-04. This surface has no refusal to test, and that is the design rather than an omission. The suite guards ONE route, POST /v1/registration-invites, which is open by necessity: an AI calls it with a person's email before that person has any account, so there is no principal to refuse. Its whole security property is the OPPOSITE of a refusal — the response must be byte-identical whether the address is new, already has an account, or already has a live invitation, because any difference turns it into an address-checking machine. The suite asserts exactly that in three tests, plus the per-address cap and single-use expiry that bound the abuse a 403 cannot. There is no second route on this router: no listing, no read, nothing an owner could reach across. A 401 or 403 added here would have to be invented. It adds and removes no refusal.

test/e2e-audio-speech.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-04. The whole surface is GET /v1/libs/aimeat-audio.js, /aimeat-speech.js and the /v1/libs index — served browser libraries, and serving them to anybody is the requirement rather than an oversight: an app running in a visitor's browser loads them by URL before that visitor has any account, and routes/libs.ts registers them with no auth middleware for exactly that reason. A 401 here would break every published app. What COULD go wrong on this surface is the file being stale or wrong, which check:sdk and check:vendored already gate, not who may read it.

test/e2e-message-transcript.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-08-16 (E2E test-quality audit, finding e2e-message-transcript:145). This surface refuses with 404, not 403, and that is deliberate: the transcribe route looks the message up as storage.getDirectMessage(id, ownerGhii), so a caller who is not a party to the message is told the message does not exist rather than that it exists and is not theirs. The suite now drives that refusal with a THIRD owner, on the plain and the force:true paths, and reads the sender's copy back afterwards to show nothing was written; the recipient reaching their OWN copy is the positive control. There is no 401 or 403 on this route to assert. test/e2e-members.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-04 — GET /v1/portfolio/members is a public list with no authenticated door on it, so 'what does a second principal get' has one answer: the same list. test/e2e-attachment-sweep.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-08, unchanged in substance since 2026-09-04. There is no door here to refuse. This suite is IN-PROCESS: it imports createServer, loadConfig and sweepReferenceAttachments directly and calls the sweep function, and it makes zero fetch() calls (measured: 0 again on this edit). What it tests is a background job deciding whether an attachment reference is retried or expired, which has no caller and therefore no principal to refuse. It does carry the refusal that IS its own — case 5 asserts that a descriptor naming a third owner's file is refused and that none of the victim's bytes reach the recipient — but that is a data-shape refusal inside the job, not a principal being turned away at a door. The HTTP doors that create those attachments live in the DM suites and carry their refusals there. Re-seeded because the suite gained case 3b (a held attachment behind 205 finished ones), which adds no HTTP call. If this ever grows one, the sha pin expires with it.

test/e2e-public-activity.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-04 — GET /v1/public/activity-feed is public by definition, and every refusal it has is content-shaped rather than principal-shaped. All of them are asserted: a PRIVATE organism does not appear, a knowledge package without catalog_listed does not appear, nothing owned by system@ reaches the ticker, and the seeded built-in skills specifically do not. Those four are the security property this feed has — an action becomes visible because it was made public, not because of who is asking — and asking as a second principal would return the identical feed. test/e2e-public-totals.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-09-04. GET /v1/public/node-totals has no refusal to test and that is the requirement rather than an omission: it powers the landing panel a visitor sees before they have an account, and the suite asserts it answers with no Authorization header at all. The question a public counter DOES raise is asked instead, and it is not status-shaped: a counter that rises when a PRIVATE organism is created tells an anonymous caller that one exists, which is the whole of what private was supposed to prevent. test/e2e-datapackage-odata.ts.reason: REVIEWED 2026-08-15: this surface has no refusal to test, and that is the design rather than an omission. An OData feed serves the rows of a PUBLISHED data package, whose CSV already sits at a permanent, world-readable /v1/pub address; putting a token in front of the feed while the file stays open would be theatre, not a control. There is therefore no second principal that gets a different answer. What the suite DOES prove instead is the fence that exists here: test 13b shows the feed is a door onto packages and cannot be steered at the owner's other storage, and tests 7-11 prove every unimplemented query construct is REFUSED (501/400) rather than ignored — which on this surface is the failure with real consequences, because an ignored $filter returns the wrong rows into somebody's report with no symptom. If the metered feed is ever built it will be a separate authenticated door, and that one owes a 401/403 case. test/e2e-mcp-install.ts.reason: Reviewed 2026-08-27, re-reviewed 2026-09-02 when the second door was added. The surface is TWO public GETs (/v1/connect/mcp.json and /v1/connect/install) that return a config file or a double-click script holding this node's MCP address and a name the caller picked. They read nothing owned by anybody, so there is no principal to refuse: 401 and 403 are not answers they can give, and asserting one would mean inventing a gate the feature does not have. Their only refusals are 400s for a client or desktop they do not know, which the suite asserts by code. The fence the doors DO have is tested instead, in 'The door tells a second principal nothing about the first': two registered owners and an unauthenticated caller must get byte-identical bytes, with neither owner's name in them. That is the failure worth catching here, because the day these routes start reflecting their caller, a door that takes no auth is handing one person's account to whoever asks next.
